Tics and Tic Disorders

classify the movement first · motor and vocal tics · Tourette criteria · tic vs compulsion · habit reversal, then medicationIs the behavior involuntary, or is it neutralizing an obsession?

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • 2 or more motor tics 1 or more vocal tics, at least 1 year, onset before 18 Tourette syndrome; echolalia counts as vocal
  • Repeated act no obsession behind it a tic, not a compulsion
  • No impairment explain and watch. Impairment CBIT (comprehensive behavioral intervention for tics) medication: a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter type 2) inhibitor such as tetrabenazine first, or an antipsychotic; an alpha-2 agonist for milder tics, especially with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder)
What it is

Sudden, rapid, nonrhythmic movements or sounds

Tourette: 2 or more motor 1 or more vocal tics for at least 1 year, onset before 18

Driver

Cause unknown runs in families (in some, dominant with incomplete penetrance)

Triggers

Family history non-modifiable male sex (about 4 boys to 1 girl) In practiceThe Merck Manual gives a different figure: a male to female ratio of 3 to 1. non-modifiable

Worse with stress fatigue downtime

Chain

Urge (in some) tic; some can hold it back for seconds to minutes

Onset typically at 4 to 6 peak at 10 to 12 lessens in adolescence a third persist for life

Insights

ADHD OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder) often impair more than the tics screen every patient

Tics ADHD an alpha-2 agonist first; a stimulant if the ADHD improves little, watching for worse tics

Mechanism and coursedetail behind the chain
Each ticSome feel an urge first; some can hold a tic back for seconds to minutes; fewer during focused tasks, usually none in sleep
ChildhoodOnset before 18, usually at 4 to 6 years; tics wax and wane
PeakMost severe at about 10 to 12 years
AdolescenceTics lessen in many
AdulthoodAbout a third resolve completely, a third improve in adolescence and adulthood, and a third have lifelong tics In practiceThe Merck Manual gives a different figure: most tics disappear on their own and about 1% persist into adulthood.
ComorbidityADHD is the most common; OCD is common too; both often interfere more than the tics; oppositional defiant disorder and autism spectrum disorder also occur
StimulantsA stimulant can bring out or worsen tics in some children, yet tics do not rule one outin trials of children with tics and ADHD, methylphenidate did not worsen tics on average
3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Tourette syndromeTwo or more motor tics plus one or more vocal tics, not always at the same time1 year or more; both motor and vocal tics
Obsessive-compulsive disorderIntrusive thoughts drive repeated acts that relieve the distressA named obsession; a tic neutralizes none. The two often coexist
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorderInattention or hyperactivity in 2 or more settings6 months or more, some before age 12; often coexists with tics
Angry or irritable mood, argument and defiance, vindictiveness6 months or more of defiance, not an involuntary movement
Persistent (chronic) tic disorderMotor or vocal tics, not both1 year or more, only one type
Provisional tic disorder (transient tic disorder)Motor and/or vocal ticsUnder 1 year
Stereotypies (stereotypic movements)Repetitive, usually bilateral, such as hand flapping; with autism or intellectual disability, or in typical young childrenRhythmic, where a tic is not; distraction, such as calling the child's name, typically stops it Also not a ticMyoclonus is sudden and nonrhythmic like a tic, but it cannot be held back and no urge comes first.
Rapid, irregular jerks, often spreading to the feet and face; may unmask OCDOften months after a strep infection; a major criterion of rheumatic fever
A drug, medication or medical causeTic-like movements with a culprit drug (eg, methylphenidate) or a condition such as seizures, Huntington disease or postviral encephalitisThe culprit drug or the other condition is found
4Workup
Why time itTelling Tourette syndrome from tics that pass may take follow-up over time. Guideline detailThe American Academy of Neurology guideline adds screening for anxiety, mood and disruptive behavior disorders, and asking about suicidal thoughts and attempts.
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Repeats exactly what other children sayEcholalia, a vocal ticCounts toward Tourette syndrome
Shrugs, turns the head, raises a hand again and again, with no obsessionMotor ticsNot OCD treatment
One tic fades and another appearsThe waxing and waning courseExpected; the diagnosis stands
Concerns reported from school aloneOnly 1 setting so farConfirm a second setting before calling it ADHD
Pause point
7-year-old referred from school for behavior; his father has OCD Offered as OCD: exposure and response prevention and an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) OCD is common alongside tics, but with no obsession his repeated acts are tics; a relative’s diagnosis does not describe this child’s movements → Tics: exposure and response prevention and an SSRI miss the target; he is bullied and isolated, so the tics impair, and treatment is warranted
5Diagnostic criteria
Defining criteria: tic disorders Tourette – two or more motor tics and one or more vocal tics, not always at the same time; tics for at least 1 year · Persistent (chronic) – motor or vocal tics, not both, for 1 year or more · Provisional – motor and/or vocal tics for less than 1 year · All three – onset before 18; not due to a medication or drug, or another medical condition (eg, seizures, Huntington disease, postviral encephalitis)
Tic types
TypeMotorVocal
Simple: brief, no social meaningBlinking, grimacing, head jerking, shoulder shruggingGrunting or barking, sniffing or snorting, throat clearing
Complex: longer, may look intentionalCombined simple tics (head turning plus shrugging); echopraxia, imitating movements; copropraxia, obscene gesturesEcholalia, repeating another person's sounds or words, or one's own; CoprolaliaSaying obscenities: only a minority of patients, socially inappropriate words
Clinical diagnosis: no test confirms it
6Severity
Treatment by impairment
SituationChoose
Tics with no functional impairmentExplain the natural history; watchful waiting
Tics that significantly interfere with activities or self-imageTreat the tics: behavioral therapy (CBIT) first
ADHD or OCD that impairsTreat it too; it often impairs more than the tics
7Treatment
1

Explainevery patient

Psychoeducation on the natural history

Without functional impairment, watchful waiting is enough. Guideline detailRefer teachers and peers to psychoeducation resources.

2

1st linetics interfere with activities or self-image

Behavioral therapy: habit reversal training, the core of What it isComprehensive behavioral intervention for tics: cognitive-behavioral therapy built around habit reversal training.Habit reversal training is the first-line treatment: tic awareness training (recognize the urge before a tic), then competing response training (a competing behavior, such as a deep breath, when the urge comes).

Offer it before medication when it is available.

3

Medicationtics still impair

A VMAT2 inhibitor such as tetrabenazine, preferred for fewer side effects; or an MechanismSecond-generation drugs block D2 dopamine and 5-HT2A serotonin receptors; aripiprazole is instead a D2 partial agonist. First-generation drugs carry significant extrapyramidal effects.Watch for drug-induced movement disorders; weight gain (risperidone, aripiprazole); ↑ prolactin from D2 blockade (haloperidol, pimozide, risperidone). Aripiprazole raises prolactin less. Pimozide or ziprasidone: an ECG (electrocardiogram) for the QTc (the interval from the Q wave to the end of the T wave, corrected for heart rate) before and after starting., aripiprazole first

Milder tics, especially with ADHD: an alpha-2 agonist, MechanismA central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist (also imidazoline receptors): lowers sympathetic outflow from the brain.Watch for sedation, low blood pressure and a slow heart rate; stopping it suddenly can cause rebound hypertension. or guanfacine, which may help both. In practiceThe Merck Manual calls oral antipsychotics (aripiprazole, haloperidol, pimozide) second-line medications for tics that are harder to control, and the 2019 American Academy of Neurology guideline calls VMAT2 inhibitors increasingly used off-label; drowsiness, depression and parkinsonism can occur.

Alpha-2 agonist: check heart rate and blood pressure; taper to stop
4

Escalatesevere tics resist these

Haloperidol or pimozide, for severe, resistant tics only

Risperidone also reduces tics but is not first line. Beyond the ladderDeep brain stimulation for an adult with severe tics after, or unable to take, several drug classes and CBIT; multidisciplinary review first.
Botulinum toxin for a localized simple motor tic in an adolescent or adult; weakness and a soft voice, all temporary.

Lowest effective dose
First treatment by situation
SituationChooseWatch for
Tics impair, no ADHDCBIT; then a Why these drugsBoth are antidopaminergic drugs, the most effective medications for tics: a VMAT2 inhibitor (tetrabenazine, valbenazine) depletes dopamine and is not linked to tardive dyskinesia or metabolic syndrome; an antipsychotic blocks dopamine receptors but carries more risk of weight gain, metabolic syndrome, dystonia and tardive dyskinesia.; Alpha-2 agonistFor less debilitating tics, with a lower risk of significant adverse effects in children; sedation and low blood pressure; weaker evidence than for antidopaminergic drugs.; if it fails and tics still impair, step up to a VMAT2 inhibitor (depletes dopamine) or an antipsychotic (blocks dopamine receptors)VMAT2 inhibitor: drowsiness, depression, parkinsonism. Antipsychotic: lowest effective dose; movement and metabolic effects. Alpha-2 agonist: heart rate, blood pressure, taper to stop
Tics impair, with ADHDCBIT; then, for milder tics, clonidine or guanfacine, which may help bothStop an alpha-2 agonist by taper: rebound hypertension
The ADHD is what impairsAn alpha-2 agonist (guanfacine or clonidine) first; may switch to a stimulant if the ADHD improves littleOn a stimulant, tics can emerge or worsen in some: watch closely; tics do not rule one out. Atomoxetine is another option
Tics with OCDCognitive-behavioral therapy (exposure and response prevention), with or without an SSRI, for the OCD; treat the tics as aboveExposure and response prevention targets compulsions; a tic neutralizes no obsession. SSRIs and tricyclics treat the OCD or depression; they play no primary role in the tics
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
Tics for under 1 yearFollow over time: that is how Tourette syndrome separates from tics that pass
Every visitExpect waxing and waning; many improve in adolescence
On an alpha-2 agonistCheck heart rate and blood pressure; taper to stop
On an antipsychotic Lowest effective dose; watch for movement, metabolic and hormonal effects; taper over weeks to months to stop
ADHD that impairsMake sure the ADHD is treated
Practice
  1. 7 yo M with head turning, shoulder shrugging and repetition of classmates' words for over a year, now bullied and socially isolated → Risperidone → Tourette syndrome that impairs him; with CBIT, a VMAT2 inhibitor such as tetrabenazine and aripiprazole not among the options, risperidone, which also reduces tics, is the best choice offered
  2. 8 yo M with mild motor and vocal tics who is performing well academically and has friends → Reassurance and education about the natural history → tics that do not impair need no tic treatment: explain the waxing and waning course and watch; habit reversal training waits until tics interfere
  3. 9 yo M with motor tics who also describes intrusive thoughts of contamination relieved only by repeated handwashing → Comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder → a tic disorder alone has no obsession behind the act; contamination thoughts relieved by handwashing are an obsession and a compulsion, treated with exposure and response prevention
  4. 7 yo M with head jerking and eye blinking for 8 months and no vocal tic → Provisional tic disorder → tics for under 1 year are provisional, whether motor, vocal or both; Tourette syndrome and persistent (chronic) tic disorder need 1 year
  5. How antipsychotic agents suppress tics in Tourette syndrome → Dopamine receptor blockade → tetrabenazine instead depletes presynaptic dopamine
  6. 8 yo with Tourette syndrome; inattention still impairs him at home and at school after a trial of guanfacine → A stimulant for the comorbid ADHD → with tics and ADHD, an alpha-2 agonist comes first; if the ADHD improves little, switch to a stimulant, watching for worse tics; stimulants are not contraindicated in Tourette syndrome: on average, methylphenidate treats the ADHD without worsening tics (American Academy of Neurology guideline, 2019), though tics can emerge or worsen in some children
  7. 7 yo with Tourette syndrome whose parents request medication to reduce the tics → Fluoxetine → a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) treats comorbid OCD, not tics
  8. 10 yo with moderate impairing tics whose parents decline an antipsychotic because of weight-gain concerns → Guanfacine → when the family declines an antipsychotic and no VMAT2 inhibitor is offered, an alpha-2 agonist is an accepted medication for tics, with fewer extrapyramidal effects
Pairs with School Difficulty in a Child is the nearest relative. It shares the same referral route, a school behavior complaint. The resolution is opposite: there the private interview reveals a learning disorder, and here the examination reveals tics. Ask: what exactly is the child doing, and is it involuntary?
Transferable rule A family history raises the prior probability, but the phenomenology decides. When a relative's diagnosis and a child's behavior are both given, first describe the behavior in neutral terms. If the behavior is sudden, rapid and nonrhythmic, with no obsession behind it, it is a tic, whatever the family carries.
Common wrong answers For a school-age child with motor and vocal tics who is referred from school and whose father has OCD: Exposure and response prevention: the father's OCD makes it tempting, but it treats compulsions driven by obsessions, and the child describes no obsession. Fluoxetine: an SSRI is a first-line medication for OCD, but it treats obsessions and compulsions, not tics. Parent management training: it treats oppositional defiant disorder, a pattern of defiance, and does nothing for involuntary movements. Methylphenidate or atomoxetine: ADHD often coexists with tics, but these movements are tics, and concerns reported from school alone do not meet the 2-setting criterion for ADHD.
